picks.title: The Flower with a Flame Inside
picks.headline: The Flower with a Flame Inside

bullets.point: Autumn arrives so gently here in eastern Maine that it can feel like late summer long after the calendar says otherwise.
bullets.detail: Autumn arrives so gently here in eastern Maine that it can feel like late summer long after the calendar says otherwise. But finally, a mid-October day comes when the sun sets before dinner, the insects cease singing, and the leaves that turned the entrance to Orono Bog into a tunnel of gold have fallen. I volunteer at the bog boardwalk on Friday afternoons, and as I make my closing circuit I look closely at the mossy hummocks beside the path. Poking through fallen leaves are the tips of Eastern skunk cabbage plants: narrow green buds a few inches high with a smaller, deep crimson-and-green streaked bud at their base. The buds are sinuously triangular and with a bit of imagination resemble flames, which is only appropriate. Eastern skunk cabbages perform an extraordinary feat of botanical heat generation.

bullets.detail: I volunteer at the bog boardwalk on Friday afternoons, and as I make my closing circuit I look closely at the mossy hummocks beside the path. Poking through fallen leaves are the tips of Eastern skunk cabbage plants: narrow green buds a few inches high with a smaller, deep crimson-and-green streaked bud at their base. The buds are sinuously triangular and with a bit of imagination resemble flames, which is only appropriate. Eastern skunk cabbages perform an extraordinary feat of botanical heat generation. Early the following spring, when skunk cabbages will be the very first wildflowers to bloom, that smallest bud will have grown into a curved sheath called a spathe—no imagination required to see the likeness of a flame—cupping a stem topped by a flower-studded, robin’s-egg-sized inflorescence that functions as a radiator. For two weeks it produces enough heat to melt a circle of bare ground in surrounding snow and reaches temperatures up to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than the still-frigid surrounding air. In the process the plant burns as much energy as a small mammal.

bullets.detail: Early the following spring, when skunk cabbages will be the very first wildflowers to bloom, that smallest bud will have grown into a curved sheath called a spathe—no imagination required to see the likeness of a flame—cupping a stem topped by a flower-studded, robin’s-egg-sized inflorescence that functions as a radiator. For two weeks it produces enough heat to melt a circle of bare ground in surrounding snow and reaches temperatures up to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than the still-frigid surrounding air. In the process the plant burns as much energy as a small mammal. “These flowers have the highest rates of energy production of any organism, including all vertebrate animals,” said Roger Seymour, a biologist at Australia’s Adelaide University who specializes in the biology of heat-producing flowers. “The only thing that comes close is the flight muscle of a bee, which has the highest rate of energy production per gram of any animal.”

bullets.point: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage.
bullets.detail: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age. No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. bullets.detail: No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest. As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power…

bullets.detail: As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state. Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.
